text: You're at a nice restaurant, scrolling through the wine list, hoping to pick the perfect bottle.
You want to enjoy a good glass without looking like you're pinching pennies, but the cheapest option feels a little too basic.
So, your eyes land on the next one up, the second-cheapest. It seems like a sensible compromise, a smart choice that balances quality and cost.
But this isn't just a happy accident; it's a clever trick called "menu anchoring." The *most* expensive wines aren't meant to be sold.
Instead, they act as a high anchor, making everything below them, especially that second-cheapest bottle, look much more reasonable by comparison.
Now you know the hidden nudge. The next time you order, you'll spot that carefully placed bottle and understand exactly why it caught your eye.
